hook.text: A delivery truck costs $60,000 and lasts five years. You don't expense it all in year one.

buildup.text: Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-lived asset across its useful life.

discovery.text: Each year, a depreciation entry reduces the asset's book value and records an expense.

twist.text: Straight-line depreciation is simplest: $60,000 ÷ 5 years = $12,000 per year.

climax.text: Without depreciation, profits would be crushed in the purchase year and inflated every year after.

punchline.text: Spread the cost. Match it to the years it helps.

quiz.question: What does straight-line depreciation do?
options: Spreads cost equally across the asset's useful life
Deducts the full cost in year one
Increases the asset's value over time

details.summary: Depreciation entries allocate the cost of long-term assets—like equipment and vehicles—over their useful life. This topic covers straight-line and accelerated depreciation methods and how to record the monthly journal entries.
details.whyItMatters: Without depreciation, the entire cost of an asset hits one period's income statement, distorting profitability. Depreciation spreads the cost fairly across all periods that benefit from the asset.
takeaways: Depreciation is a non-cash expense that reduces the book value of assets over time
Straight-line depreciation spreads the cost evenly; accelerated methods front-load it
The entry debits Depreciation Expense and credits Accumulated Depreciation every period

faq.question: What is depreciation in bookkeeping?
faq.answer: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of a long-term asset's cost over its useful life. A $10,000 machine expected to last 5 years would generate $2,000 in annual depreciation expense under the straight-line method, reducing its book value gradually.

faq.question: Why is depreciation called a non-cash expense?
faq.answer: No cash leaves the business when depreciation is recorded—the cash was spent when the asset was purchased. Depreciation is an accounting allocation that spreads that original cost across future periods, reducing reported profit without affecting actual cash flow.
